What happens when the 5G lane corrections stop?

Pick a speed, a road, a gyro, and an outage length, then play the outage. Five trigger policies drive the same nonlinear vehicle through the same outage and the same worst-case disturbances; only the moment they decide to brake differs. Our method is the certified trigger, highlighted in blue.

The 64 evaluation routes of the CICV5G dataset, replayed with their measured round-trip times. Every time the corrections go stale, each policy decides when to brake; the certified deadline changes from outage to outage, the fixed timeout does not. Speed is governed to stay inside the certifiable domain, as in the paper's replay.

All 64 evaluation routes, 37 km

Totals over every evaluation route of the replay, for the 0.2 deg/s gyro and the outages selected below. Departures inside the certifiable domain are the paper's main comparison.

One route at a time

Every outage on this route

Information age is the time since the last accepted correction. A policy brakes when the age reaches its trigger; an outage that ends earlier is ridden through.

A stop is not needed if riding through the whole outage would have kept the lane. Simulations use the nonlinear single-track vehicle with tire saturation, load transfer, a 0.09–0.11 s steering delay, and errors held at their adverse limits. The certified trigger brakes at the deadline certified for the detection state; outside the certifiable domain it stops at once. The TLC trigger brakes when the time-to-line-crossing of the estimated corners drops below 6 s, the most cautious threshold tried on the calibration routes.
